stories.title: Haze Gets Worse: Sarawak Declares Emergency, New Fires Threaten Indonesia's New Capital
stories.headline_kid: The haze in our region just got a lot worse — Sarawak is having its worst smoky air since 2019, and new fires are burning near Indonesia's brand-new capital city!
summary: Haze is smoky, hazy air that happens when forests are burnt down, usually to clear land for farming. This smoke can travel very far on the wind, sometimes crossing into other countries. Right now, Sarawak, a state in Malaysia on the island of Borneo, is having its worst haze since 2019.

People in Sarawak say they feel 'worried' and 'confused' because the haze is affecting daily life. Some businesses have had to close early, and the state government has declared an emergency to deal with the problem.

At the same time, new wildfires have started spreading near Nusantara, Indonesia's new capital city that is still being built. The biggest fire has already burnt about 300 hectares of forest — that's roughly the size of 400 football fields! Officials are asking for cloud seeding (making it rain artificially) and water-bombing (dropping water from planes) to put out the flames.
Singapore has already had unhealthy air recently because of similar fires. If the wind shifts, our skies could get hazy again too, so it's worth keeping an eye on the news.

lenses.me: If the haze drifts to Singapore, you might need to stay indoors during recess or PE lessons.
lenses.family: Your family may need to keep air purifiers ready and check the PSI (air quality) index before outdoor outings.
lenses.friends: Classmates in Malaysia and Indonesia might have their outdoor school activities cancelled because of the smoky air.
lenses.nation: Singapore keeps monitoring the haze situation closely and has standby plans, like distributing masks, in case our air turns unhealthy again.
lenses.world: This shows how fires in one country can affect the health and daily lives of people in neighbouring countries, which is why countries need to work together to stop it.

stories.title: 52 Singaporeans Arrested in China Over a Money Scheme
stories.headline_kid: 52 Singaporeans got in trouble in China for joining a scheme that promised easy money — but it turned out to be against the law.
summary: 52 Singaporeans were arrested in Guangxi, China, because they were allegedly involved in a pyramid scheme. A pyramid scheme is like a chain: people are told they'll get rich by getting other people to join and pay money, but only the few people at the very top actually make money.

Almost everyone else who joins ends up losing what they paid in, because there's no real product being sold — just more people being recruited. This kind of scheme is illegal in many countries, including China and Singapore, because it tricks people out of their savings.

Lawyers in China explained that punishments depend on how involved a person was. Someone who organised the scheme could face a much heavier penalty than someone who simply joined without knowing much about it.
This case is a good reminder for families to be careful of 'get-rich-quick' offers, whether online or from friends. If something sounds too good to be true, it usually is.

lenses.me: You'll learn to recognise 'get-rich-quick' tricks so you don't get fooled when you're older.
lenses.family: This reminds your family to be extra careful about investment offers from friends or online strangers.
lenses.friends: You might hear parents or older relatives talking about this case at home or online.
lenses.nation: Singapore works closely with other countries like China to protect citizens from scams, even when they happen overseas.
lenses.world: It shows that scams don't stay in one country — they can involve people from many places, so countries need to cooperate to stop them.

stories.title: Ships Attacked Near Iran: Why It Could Affect Petrol Prices Here
stories.headline_kid: American and Iranian forces fired at ships near Iran over the weekend — and that far-away conflict could actually affect prices in Singapore.
summary: On Saturday, US and Iranian forces fired at ships in the waters near Iran. Three Iranian oil tankers (huge ships that carry oil) were struck by the Americans, and Iran said it targeted three other tankers travelling on 'unauthorised routes'. This is part of a conflict that has been building up since February.

Iran is a country with a lot of oil, and oil tankers from that region travel all over the world, including through waters near Singapore. When there is fighting near important oil routes, it becomes riskier and more expensive to move oil around.

Singapore doesn't produce much oil of its own — we buy and trade it from other countries. If oil becomes more expensive or harder to transport because of conflicts like this, prices for petrol, cooking gas and even electricity in Singapore can go up too.
Singapore is also one of the world's busiest ports, so any trouble that makes shipping more dangerous or costly matters a lot to our economy.

lenses.me: You might hear grown-ups talk about rising petrol or transport costs because of news like this.
lenses.family: Your family's petrol, cooking gas or electricity bills could be affected if oil prices rise.
lenses.friends: Classmates' families who drive or run businesses using fuel might feel the pinch too.
lenses.nation: Singapore's economy depends on stable oil trade and safe shipping routes, so our government watches these events closely.
lenses.world: It shows how a conflict in one part of the world can ripple out and affect prices and businesses everywhere, including places far from the fighting.

stories.title: Malaysia's Leaders Debate: Should Elections Come Early?
stories.headline_kid: Malaysia's leaders are arguing about whether to hold their next big election earlier than planned — and that matters to Singapore too.
summary: Malaysia's Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim said he is open to considering an early general election, after several leaders — including his own deputy prime minister — called for a 'snap poll'. A general election is when citizens vote to choose their government, similar to how Singapore holds its own elections.
A 'snap poll' means holding the election sooner than the usual schedule, which is currently expected around 2027. Anwar said any final decision would only be made after careful thought.
Malaysia is Singapore's closest neighbour, connected by the Causeway and the new RTS Link train. Many Singaporean families cross the border regularly for holidays, groceries, or work.
Changes in Malaysia's government can affect things Singaporeans care about, like food prices, water agreements, and cross-border travel plans, so it's worth paying attention to.

lenses.me: If your family visits Johor Bahru often, changes in Malaysia's government could affect your trips.
lenses.family: Grocery prices for food imported from Malaysia could be affected by political changes there.
lenses.friends: Some classmates' parents might work across the border, so this news could matter to their families too.
lenses.nation: Singapore keeps a close eye on Malaysia's politics because of our shared history, trade, and infrastructure projects like the RTS Link.
lenses.world: This shows how elections in one country can have effects that reach beyond its own borders, especially for close neighbours.

stories.title: Meet the Singaporean Behind One of Asia's Best Bars
stories.headline_kid: A Singaporean bartender just won some of the biggest awards in the world for his craft — and he's not stopping there!
summary: Indra Kantono, co-founder of Singapore's famous bar Jigger & Pony, has had an amazing year. In July, he was named Best International Bar Mentor at the Spirited Awards, and soon after he won the Roku Industry Icon Award at Asia's 50 Best Bars.

For 14 years, Indra has been building bars and training young bartenders in Singapore. His work has helped put our small country on the map as a top destination for cocktails (fancy mixed drinks) — much like how a coach helps a whole team become champions.

He is now expanding his business into Jakarta, Indonesia, and thinking about how Singapore's drink and hospitality scene can grow beyond just serving drinks — perhaps by teaching more skills to young people in the industry.
Indra's story shows how Singaporeans can become world-class experts in creative fields, and how passion, hard work, and mentoring others can lead to big success.

lenses.me: It shows that following a passion — even one like mixing drinks — can turn into a world-class career.
lenses.family: Your family might enjoy visiting cocktail bars (or mocktail bars for kids!) as part of exploring Singapore's food and drink scene when you're older.
lenses.friends: You and your friends can talk about how Singapore is becoming known worldwide for more than just food — even drinks!
lenses.nation: Achievements like this add to Singapore's reputation as a global hub for food, drinks and hospitality.
lenses.world: Indra's expansion into Jakarta shows how Singapore's creative businesses are influencing and connecting with the wider region.
